meta.audience: Zeezrom, and the people of Ammonihah

world_behind.title: Alma speaks to one man in front of a crowd
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has him addressing Zeezrom, and verse 2 notes that the multitude was great and heard all of it. Verse 5 makes the arrangement explicit: what he says to Zeezrom he says to all. The chapter is a private conversation staged in public, and both audiences are being worked.

world_behind.title: The questioner has changed sides
world_behind.text: Zeezrom opened the last chapter buying a denial and closes this one asking for more. Verse 8 says he "began to inquire of them diligently" (v. 8). Diligence is the same word the chapter will use for how revelation is measured out. The man who set the trap is now the model of the doctrine being taught.

cites.quote: began to inquire of them diligently

spans.text: began to inquire of them diligently

world_behind.title: Antionah asks in good faith
world_behind.text: A chief ruler raises the cherubim and the flaming sword of Eden as a scriptural objection to endless life, and it is a real argument from a text he knows. Alma does not dismiss it. He says it is the thing he was about to explain, and spends fourteen verses on it.

world_behind.title: Eden is being read as a matter of law
world_behind.text: The argument in verses 23 and 26 turns on whether God's word would have held. Had Adam reached the tree of life after the sentence of death, the word would have been void. The chapter treats the garden as a case in which a promise had to be kept.

world_behind.title: Psalm 95 is under this whole sermon
world_behind.text: The provocation and the rest, the swearing in wrath, the hardening of hearts: all of it is the language of the psalm the Israelites sang about the wilderness generation, and the letter to the Hebrews would later build on the same passage. Alma preaches it to a city about to be destroyed.

world_behind.title: Chains run through the chapter
world_behind.text: The adversary encircles with chains (v. 6), ignorance becomes "the chains of hell" (v. 11), and the unrepentant are chained down to destruction (v. 17). One image carries the argument from a courtroom trick to a doctrine of damnation.

world_behind.title: The record's fullest account of the Fall so far
world_behind.text: Lehi taught it to Jacob two hundred years earlier in different terms. Here it arrives as an answer to a hostile question in a doomed city, and it is the version the rest of the book will build on.

words.text: Craft, the skill of the indirect. Alma calls Zeezrom's plan subtle "as to the subtlety of the devil" (v. 4), and the King James Bible attaches the older spelling of the adjective to exactly one famous creature: the serpent, more subtil than any beast of the field. The word choice identifies whose method was being used before the chapter identifies whose plan it was.

cites.quote: as to the subtlety of the devil

spans.text: as to the subtlety of the devil

words.text: A measured share, the amount allotted to one person. The doctrine in verses 9 through 11 makes revelation a quantity that moves: harden the heart and "the same receiveth the lesser portion of the word" (v. 10), soften it and the portion grows until the mysteries are known in full. Nothing here is described as withheld arbitrarily. The supply tracks the appetite.

cites.quote: the same receiveth the lesser portion of the word

spans.text: the same receiveth the lesser portion of the word

words.text: Gladly, willingly, and in older use with a note of desperation. It occurs once in this record and twice in the King James Bible, where a starving prodigal would fain have filled his belly with husks. Alma uses it for what the condemned would gladly do: "we would fain be glad" (v. 14) to have the mountains fall on them. The word carries the wish of someone with no better option.

On trial, under test, with the outcome not yet fixed. The word is absent from the King James Bible and enters this record here, in the claim that "this life became a probationary state" (v. 24). Alma will reach for it three more times when he explains justice to his son thirty chapters later. A probation implies a term with an end and a judge already appointed.

cites.quote: this life became a probationary state

spans.text: this life became a probationary state

words.text: Serving to get ready for something else. Its companion word, and the pair does the chapter's work: probation is the test, preparation is the point. Alma says our first parents partaking of the tree of life would have left them "having no preparatory state" (v. 26), and that makes the flaming sword an act of mercy.

An act that rouses anger, and in the psalms a proper noun for one particular rebellion in the wilderness. Treated at Jacob 1:7. Alma warns against wrath coming down "as in the first provocation" (v. 36) and pairs it with entering into rest, the exact pairing of Psalm 95. He is reading a city its own history in borrowed words.

phrases.text: Alma opens by upgrading the charge Amulek made. The lie was told to a man and the offense is against God, because the thoughts behind it were already known. What the charge establishes is that Zeezrom was never hidden.

phrases.term: Encircle you about with his chains
phrases.text: The first of the chapter's three chain images. Encircling is patient work, done from the outside, and the verb suggests something closing gradually. Alma applies it to a plan Zeezrom thought was his own.

phrases.term: It is given unto many to know the mysteries of God
phrases.text: The sentence that opens the chapter's central doctrine, and it begins with generosity. Many are given to know. The restriction that follows falls on imparting, and it is calibrated to the hearer.

phrases.term: The lesser portion of the word
phrases.text: Revelation described as a quantity that rises and falls. This is the chapter's most practical claim: a person's access to God's word is responsive to what that person does with the last portion. The mechanism runs in both directions and the verse states both.

phrases.term: This is what is meant by the chains of hell
phrases.text: Alma stops to define a phrase, which he rarely does. The chains turn out to be knowing nothing of the mysteries, arrived at by hardening until there is nothing left to harden. Hell's restraint, in this account, is ignorance a person chose.

phrases.term: We would fain be glad if we could command the rocks and the mountains to fall upon us
phrases.text: The wish to be hidden, phrased as a wish for weight. John's Revelation would put the same words in the mouths of kings at the last day, and Hosea before him. Alma gives the line to everyone whose thoughts have condemned them, which by verse 14 includes his hearers.

phrases.term: Acknowledge to our everlasting shame that all his judgments are just
phrases.text: The hardest sentence in the judgment passage. Nobody argues at the bar. The condemned agree, out loud, and the agreement is itself the shame. Nothing in the scene requires a prosecution.

phrases.term: A second death, which is a spiritual death
phrases.text: The definition arrives in the middle of a sentence and the chapter builds the rest of its argument on it. Temporal death is what Amulek already covered. This one is dying "as to things pertaining unto righteousness" (v. 16), a death a living person can be inside.

cites.quote: as to things pertaining unto righteousness

spans.text: as to things pertaining unto righteousness

phrases.text: The stakes of the Eden argument, stated bluntly. If Adam had reached the tree of life after being told "thou shalt surely die," the sentence would have failed. Alma's defense of the flaming sword is that God's word had to hold, and the whole plan of redemption depends on its holding.

phrases.term: This life became a probationary state
phrases.text: The turn from problem to purpose. The Fall produced death, and the space between the Fall and death is reframed as a term of trial. Everything the record says later about repentance rests on there being time.

phrases.term: These shall enter into my rest
phrases.text: The promise, quoted as God's own speech. Rest here is a place a person arrives at by not hardening, and the next verse gives its opposite in an oath. Psalm 95:7–11 makes the same promise and the same threat in the same order.
The warning that dates itself. Alma assumes his hearers know which provocation was first and what it cost, and he tells them a second one is under way. The city had about a year left.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: A private answer delivered to a crowd
verses.text: Alma opens his mouth to speak to one man, and verse 2 records who actually heard it: "the words that Alma spake unto Zeezrom were heard by the people round about; for the multitude was great." The record fixes the audience before the argument starts, and verse 5 then makes the widening explicit, "what I say unto thee I say unto all."

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: The chapter's governing word belongs to the devil first
verses.text: Plan is used ten times here, which is more than in any other chapter of scripture. The first three uses are not doctrinal: "thy plan was a very subtle plan," and "this was a plan of thine adversary." Before the word can carry redemption it is made to carry a trap, and the reader meets it as something an enemy assembles.

verses.label: v. 8
verses.title: The man who came to trap them asks for an exposition
verses.text: Zeezrom's question is not his own material: "What does this mean which Amulek hath spoken concerning the resurrection of the dead?" He quotes the other missionary back and asks what it meant. The record has the interrogator become a student without narrating the change, and supplies only his trembling as evidence.

verses.label: v. 9–11
verses.title: One rule, stated forward and then run backwards
verses.text: Verse 10 gives it in the positive direction, harden the heart and receive the lesser portion, refuse to harden and receive the greater until the mysteries are known in full. Verse 11 then walks the other way to its end: lesser portion, until they know nothing, then captivity. The record does not argue the rule. It states it, reverses it, and names the result.

verses.label: v. 25
verses.title: The word changes hands
verses.text: From this verse onward every remaining use of plan is the plan of redemption, at verses 25, 26, 30, 32 and 33. The term that opened the chapter as the adversary's subtlety finishes it as the thing laid from the foundation of the world. Nothing in the chapter remarks on the transfer.

verses.label: v. 36–37
verses.title: The doctrine turns into an imperative
verses.text: The closing verses put the rule of verses 10 and 11 into the second person and then the first: if ye will harden your hearts ye shall not enter into the rest of the Lord, and then "let us repent, and harden not our hearts." Alma ends by including himself in the instruction, and the last thing the chapter does is stop explaining and start asking.

chapter.title: The doctrine is produced by a hostile room
chapter.text: Zeezrom set out to destroy a witness and ended by asking the question at verse 8 that produces the record's fullest account of the Fall, probation, and rest. The sermon runs from verse 9 to verse 37, twenty-nine verses, and every one of them is answering a hostile questioner rather than instructing a congregation.

chapter.title: Revelation is described as responsive
chapter.text: Verses 9 through 11 make the amount a person receives depend on what they did with the last amount. It explains why two people can sit through the same sermon and leave with different quantities, and it puts the variable in the hearer.

chapter.title: The chapter defines its own terms
chapter.text: Four terms are defined inside the sermon: the chains of hell at verse 11, "a second death, which is a spiritual death" at verse 16, "this life became a probationary state" at verse 24, and a "preparatory state" at verse 26. Alma 11 has just spent forty verses arguing over the meaning of words and coins, and the answer here is to fix meanings rather than to win points.

chapter.title: A good question gets a long answer
chapter.text: Antionah is identified as "a chief ruler among them" and his objection at verses 20 and 21 is quoted at length, including the scripture he cites, "God placed cherubim and a flaming sword on the east of the garden of Eden." The reply runs from verse 22 to verse 27. The record could have made an Ammonihahite ruler ridiculous; instead it gives him the citation and the reasoning and answers him on his own ground.

chapter.title: The flaming sword is read as mercy
chapter.text: Verse 23 states the alternative outcome as a reduction to absurdity: had Adam eaten of the tree of life "there would have been no death, and the word would have been void, making God a liar." Verse 26 runs it the other way, that they "would have been forever miserable, having no preparatory state." The flaming sword of Genesis 3:24 is thus read twice as the thing that made repentance possible, and the argument reaches that conclusion without adding anything to the Genesis text.

chapter.title: Commandments come after knowledge
chapter.text: Verses 28 through 32 put the order plainly: God appointed, then told, then commanded. The sequence matters to a book that keeps insisting people are judged according to the light they had.

chapter.title: The sermon ends inside Psalm 95
chapter.text: Provocation, hardening, wrath, rest, an oath sworn. Alma hands a Nephite city the psalm Israel sang about the generation that died in the wilderness, and the city is about a year from its own destruction.

applications.title: Know who is actually listening
applications.text: Alma opened his mouth to answer one man and the record immediately says who heard it, "the words that Alma spake unto Zeezrom were heard by the people round about." Verse 5 then makes it explicit, "what I say unto thee I say unto all." Before you say the private version of something in a room, decide whether you would say it to the room.

applications.title: Watch the word you inherited from the other side
applications.text: Plan enters the chapter as the adversary's, "thy plan was a very subtle plan," and leaves it as the plan of redemption, with no comment on the transfer. A word can be reclaimed. Notice which of your own vocabulary you are still using in somebody else's sense.

applications.title: Notice which way your portion is moving
applications.text: The doctrine says the amount you receive tracks what you did with the last amount, and verse 11 runs the same rule down to nothing. Compare what you understand now against a year ago; the direction is more diagnostic than the level.

applications.title: Define the word before you argue about it
applications.text: Alma stops to say what the chains of hell actually means, and the chapter defines three more terms as it goes. In your next disagreement that keeps circling, name what one contested word means to you and ask what it means to them before going further.

applications.title: Answer the good question at length
applications.text: Antionah objected from scripture and Alma gave him fourteen verses. When someone raises a real difficulty, the respectful response is proportion. Short answers to serious questions communicate that the question was not serious.

applications.title: Test a reading by supposing the other one
applications.text: Alma checks the flaming sword twice by running the alternative: no death and the word made void, or life forever with "no preparatory state." If a restriction in your life looks like pure exclusion, work out what would have followed without it.

applications.title: Treat the interval as a term
applications.text: The space between now and death is described as a probation with a purpose. Pick one thing you have been treating as something to get through, and ask what it would look like if it were the test itself.

applications.title: Expect the instruction after the information
applications.text: The order is appointed, then made known, then commanded. Nobody in this account is held to a rule they were not first told about. When you are responsible for someone, put the explaining before the requiring.

questions.text: What have I told myself was a private calculation that was never actually private?
When did I last inquire diligently about something I had previously been arguing against, and what changed first?
What did I do with the last clear thing I was given, and does that explain how much has come since?
If my words, works and thoughts each testified separately, which of the three would I least want called?
What true judgment about myself would I agree with out loud and still be ashamed of?
If this stretch of my life is the test rather than the wait, what am I actually being tested on?
What is the provocation I have already been through once, and am I walking into it again?
